interviewQuestions.question: What actually causes an ANR, and why does it matter that Android uses a single main thread for UI work?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
An ANR fires when the main thread has been unable to process a pending input event or certain system callbacks for too long — roughly five seconds for input dispatch, shorter for some Broadcast Receiver callbacks. The reason this is even possible is that Android processes all UI work — layout, drawing, input handling — through a single main thread pulling messages off a queue one at a time, with no preemption inside that model: whatever's at the front of the queue runs to completion before anything behind it, including a user's tap, gets a chance.

The key thing I'd emphasize: it doesn't matter whether the blocking cause is one very slow synchronous call (a blocking network request, a large file read) or many smaller operations that individually look fine but add up past the threshold — from the watchdog's perspective, both look identical: the thing at the front of the queue has been running too long while something's waiting behind it.

The practical consequence for how you write Android code: anything that can take a meaningful amount of time — I/O, heavy computation, anything not guaranteed to be fast — has to run off the main thread, via a coroutine on `Dispatchers.IO`/`Default`, or it becomes an ANR candidate the instant it's slow enough, on a slow enough device, at the wrong moment. This is the same underlying constraint that makes `onCreate` performance and `onBindViewHolder` performance matter so much elsewhere in Android — it's all the same single thread being protected.

**Testing:** whether you understand the mechanism (single-threaded message queue, no preemption) rather than just knowing "don't block the main thread" as a rule without the reason behind it.

interviewQuestions.question: A production crash dashboard shows a slow, steady rise in out-of-memory crashes over several release cycles, with no single obvious cause. How would you investigate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A slow rise over multiple releases, rather than a sudden spike after one specific release, points toward an accumulating leak that's been getting slightly worse with each change rather than one clear regression — I'd start by pulling in leak-detection tooling (LeakCanary or equivalent) across the app's main flows if it isn't already running continuously in debug/QA builds, since that's the fastest way to surface *which* objects are actually surviving past when they should.

I'd specifically look for the two classic shapes: a static field holding an Activity or View directly, and — the subtler one — an anonymous inner class or lambda registered with something long-lived (a system service, a static callback registry) that implicitly captures its enclosing Activity, invisible in the class's own source text. I'd check recent PRs for new listener/callback registrations specifically, since a missing unregister call produces zero functional symptom on its own — the feature keeps working — so it's exactly the kind of change that ships silently and only shows up as a slow-burning memory trend weeks or releases later.

Once leak-detection tooling flags specific objects, I'd trace the actual reference chain it reports rather than guessing — it typically shows the exact path ("X is held by Y's field, which is registered with Z") which turns "there's a leak somewhere" into a specific line of code to fix, usually a missing `onDestroy`/`onStop` unregister call paired with the registration that was added.

I'd also connect this to the memory-pressure-causes-ANRs relationship: if the same releases also show a slight uptick in ANRs correlated with longer app sessions, that's supporting evidence the accumulated leaked memory is degrading GC behavior broadly, not just risking an eventual OOM — worth mentioning specifically because it means fixing the leak likely also improves an ANR metric that looked unrelated on the surface.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a vague, slow-trending production symptom to a specific investigative process using real tooling, rather than guessing at a single cause.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you decide whether an object leak-detection tooling flags is a real bug or a legitimate long-lived cache, and what would you do differently for each?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The decision hinges on two questions: was this reference held **intentionally**, and is it **bounded**? A legitimate cache is deliberately designed to hold data longer than a single screen's lifetime, and a well-designed one has a size or count cap with an eviction policy — it's holding data on purpose, for a reason, with a limit. An actual leak is the opposite on both axes: nobody intended for the reference to be held this long, and there's no bound at all — it just accumulates for as long as the app runs.

The other distinguishing signal is *what* is being held. A cache holding raw data (bitmaps, parsed objects, API responses) is a normal design choice. Tooling flagging an Activity, View, or Context instance specifically — something tied to a UI lifecycle — surviving past its own destruction is the actual leak signature, because there's essentially never a legitimate reason to intentionally hold a destroyed Activity alive; that's not a caching strategy, it's always a bug.

For a confirmed leak, the fix is finding and breaking the unintended reference — usually a missing unregister call or an inner class handed to something longer-lived. For a legitimate cache that tooling nonetheless flags (which can happen if it doesn't yet have a bound), I wouldn't treat the flag itself as the bug — I'd instead evaluate separately whether the cache actually needs a size cap, which is a distinct, lower-urgency conversation about resource usage rather than a leak fix.

I'd specifically warn a team against reflexively "fixing" every object that survives longer than one screen — that wastes effort chasing legitimate design decisions and can even lead to accidentally breaking a cache that was working as intended.

**Testing:** whether you can apply nuanced judgment to a tooling signal rather than treating every flagged object as an automatic bug to eliminate.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Debugging Judgment

interviewQuestions.question: As a staff engineer, what process would you put in place to prevent Context leaks and ANRs from recurring across a large team, rather than fixing them one at a time as they're reported?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd focus on catching both classes of bug close to when they're introduced, because both share the same property: they produce no immediate functional symptom, so they ship silently and are only discovered much later, far from the change that caused them, when they're far more expensive to trace.

For leaks specifically: running leak-detection tooling continuously in debug and QA builds, not just occasionally when someone remembers to check, so a new leak surfaces within the same development cycle as the change that introduced it, while the responsible diff is still fresh in everyone's memory. I'd also add a review checklist item — every new listener/callback registration requires an explicit, visible unregister counterpart in the same diff, checked as a required review question, since a missing unregister produces zero test failure on its own.

For ANRs: I'd want automated performance testing that specifically measures main-thread blocking time for critical user flows, not just crash-free rate, since a growing pile of "acceptable" main-thread work can push a flow toward the ANR threshold gradually with no single change obviously responsible — this needs a trend metric, not just a pass/fail gate. I'd also push for any new synchronous or blocking API usage (a legacy library call, a file operation) to require an explicit justification for why it's safe to call on the calling thread, rather than assuming safety by default.

Beyond process, I'd invest in making the safe path the easy path: shared utilities for lifecycle-scoped registration/unregistration (so the pairing happens automatically rather than by discipline alone), and lint rules or static analysis flagging the specific shapes covered here — inner classes captured into long-lived registries, static fields typed as `Activity`/`Context`/`View` — so the most common mistake patterns get caught at build time rather than depending on every individual engineer remembering the theory.

**Testing:** whether you can design systemic prevention rather than relying on individual vigilance for bug classes that specifically produce no immediate symptom when introduced.
